column4: After the barrier opens, people surge over one another, يَمُوجُ فِي بَعْضٍ, as the trumpet is blown and all are gathered. This is the section’s dictionary root د ك ك crowding image in a final-day scene, with chaotic waves as a contrast to ordered rows; 18:100 then displays Hell.

People follow the Caller on that Day with no deviation, and their voices are humbled; 20:107 describes the level plain they cross. The verse adds directed, orderly movement toward a summons beside the section’s arrival in rows.

The criminals see the Fire and know they are about to fall into it, finding no escape. This gives the section’s exposed Hell a specific human response: recognition that its appearance means their unavoidable destination.
Each person will come to the Merciful on Resurrection Day alone, فَرْدًا. This individual arrival is a specific counter-image to the section’s collective rows of angels.

On the day each soul comes pleading for itself and is repaid for what it did, arrival leads directly to personal accounting. It complements the section’s arrival scene with what that encounter requires of each person.

The earth and heavens are replaced, and all come before God, the One, the Irresistible. This joins the section’s transformed ground to the arrival before the Lord, while depicting a cosmic remaking rather than a flattened surface.

When wrongdoers see the angels, the verse says there is no good news for them that day; 25:25 continues with the sky splitting and angels descending. It supplies the fearful human side of the angelic appearance in the section.

Gog and Magog are released and rush down from every elevation; this gives the section’s dictionary sense of د ك ك as a crowd surging over something a distinct end-time mass movement, chaotic rather than in ranks.
This list names Noah’s people, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh before the next verse names Thamud and other factions. Its own contribution is to repeat the section’s sequence of named earlier communities.
Thamud, Lot’s people, and the dwellers of the thicket continue the preceding list of earlier factions in 38:12; Thamud directly overlaps the section’s succession of punished peoples.

The verse lists ʿĀd, Thamud, the people of al-Rass, and many generations between them. This is another explicit chain of communities like the section’s remembered sequence of ʿĀd, Thamud, and Pharaoh.

The people of Noah, the companions of al-Rass, and Thamud are named as earlier deniers; 50:13 continues the chain with ʿĀd and Pharaoh. Its own list repeats two peoples in the section’s historical sequence.

This verse names ʿĀd, Pharaoh, and Lot’s people among those before; 50:12 precedes it with Noah’s people and Thamud, and 50:14 concludes that these groups denied messengers and the threat came true. It repeats the section’s succession of former peoples.

The verse says the people of the thicket and Tubbaʿ denied the messengers, so the threat came true; 50:12–13 supply the preceding series, including Thamud, ʿĀd, and Pharaoh. It completes a parallel chain of rejected communities and judgment.

The section’s secondary dictionary form of ف ج ر describes calamities bursting over a people; here opponents demand that a spring be made to burst from the earth. This is a concrete counter-sense of the root, continued by the demand for rivers in 17:91.
The demand is for rivers to gush through a garden, using the section’s root ف ج ر in a provision scene rather than its dictionary image of sudden calamity; 17:90 gives the preceding spring demand.

When the command comes, the town is overturned and stones rain down on it. This is a specific sudden, cascading punishment of a people like the section’s secondary dictionary image of disasters bursting upon them.
The town is overturned and stones of baked clay rain down upon its people. This repeats the sudden destructive onslaught described in the section’s secondary dictionary sense of ف ج ر.

The people of Lot are rained upon, and the verse calls it a rain for the criminals. This is another concrete cascading punishment of a community alongside the section’s dictionary image of calamities bursting upon people.
A rain is poured on Lot’s people and described as a terrible rain for those warned. This repeats the section’s specific image of sudden calamity descending on a people.
